```{r, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

A fitted direction answers only part of a regression question. Before using
standard errors or comparing models, check which probability model was fitted,
whether a finite optimum was reached, and which observations the comparison
uses. This guide follows those decisions on a reproducible example.

## Prepare observations with a known model

The response below follows a homogeneous von Mises model. The target direction
`x2` contributes with coefficient 0.35 and modifier `z2`; `x1` is the reference.

```{r}
library(CircularRegression)

set.seed(20260530)
n <- 200
x1 <- runif(n, -pi, pi)
x2 <- runif(n, -pi, pi)
z2 <- runif(n, 0.2, 1.8)
mu <- atan2(
  sin(x1) + 0.35 * z2 * sin(x2),
  cos(x1) + 0.35 * z2 * cos(x2)
)
error <- as.numeric(circular::rvonmises(n, circular::circular(0), kappa = 3))
dat <- data.frame(y = atan2(sin(mu + error), cos(mu + error)), x1, x2, z2)

fit <- circular_regression(y ~ x1 + x2:z2, dat, reference = "x1")
fit$convergence
fit$fit_status
fit$inference_available
fit$score_norm
```

A small score is a numerical stopping condition. It does not prove that an
angular objective has only one maximum. The homogeneous objective can have
several stationary points, especially with diffuse errors; compare suitable
initial values when the scientific conclusion depends on the fitted optimum.

## Extract uncertainty on the fitted scale

The common interface delegates covariance to its final fitted model. In the
two-step workflow, this is the homogeneous fit. The consensus step is an
initialization, not an additional source of variability added to its covariance.

```{r}
coef(fit)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, robust = TRUE)))
```

The first covariance uses the homogeneous von Mises model. The sandwich uses
independent observation scores. Neither corrects serial dependence or
within-animal clustering. Use `angular_re()` for the documented random-intercept
model when there are repeated observations within independent groups.

## Compare nested homogeneous models

The reduced model removes the target direction. Both fits use exactly the same
observations and the same reference coefficient and sign.

```{r}
full <- angular(y ~ x1 + x2:z2, dat, reference = "x1")
reduced <- angular(y ~ x1, dat, reference = "x1")
angular_lrtest(full, reduced)
```

The T2 statistic tests the additional homogeneous coefficient under regular,
identifiable models with independent errors. It does not compare a homogeneous
model with a consensus model. A term `x:z` is ordered in this interface: `x`
is a direction and `z` is its modifier. Reversing those roles changes the mean
construction even if R prints the same interaction label after reordering.

## Distinguish error constructions with information criteria

The consensus model estimates one coefficient per directional term and lets
the concentration vary with resultant length. Its coefficients are not on the
same scale as the normalized homogeneous coefficient.

```{r}
fit_consensus <- circular_regression(y ~ x1 + x2:z2, dat, method = "consensus")
coef(fit_consensus)
AIC(fit, fit_consensus)
BIC(fit, fit_consensus)
```

These information criteria use the same responses, likelihood constants and
angular measure. They compare probability models, not two estimates of an
identical coefficient. They require finite converged fits. With arbitrary case
weights, ordinary unweighted likelihood interpretations do not carry over; the
weighted BIC convention uses the number of retained rows.

## Read circular residual diagnostics

The `ggcircular` rose compares the residual distribution with the fitted von
Mises bin expectation. The fitted-direction plot shows whether residuals
vary systematically across the fitted angles.

```{r residual-rose, eval=requireNamespace("ggcircular", quietly=TRUE), fig.alt="Circular rose and kernel density of the simulated fit residuals with a fitted von Mises reference."}
plot(fit, type = "rose", bins = 12)
```

```{r fitted-residuals, eval=requireNamespace("ggcircular", quietly=TRUE), fig.alt="Wrapped residuals against fitted direction, with axes in radians."}
plot(fit, type = "fitted")
```

Use the PIT Q-Q plot to compare fitted-distribution probabilities with uniform
quantiles and the index plot to check for changes over observation order.

```{r probability-and-index-diagnostics, eval=FALSE}
plot(fit, type = "pit")
plot(fit, type = "index")
```

Curvature can suggest a distributional mismatch, but the diagonal is descriptive
because the same observations estimated the parameters. A concentrated rose
alone is not evidence of independence.

A useful response to a pattern is to inspect the implicated records and
covariates, then assess a scientifically motivated change to the model.
Increasing the number of optimizer iterations cannot resolve a mismatched
error distribution or an omitted dependence structure.

## Recognize a fit without a finite maximum

If all responses coincide with a single explanatory direction, concentration
can increase without reaching a finite maximum. Some consensus terms can have
the same issue when their modifiers are zero for the remaining observations.

```{r}
aligned <- data.frame(y = rep(0, 10), reference = 0)
boundary_fit <- consensus(y ~ reference, aligned)
boundary_fit$fit_status
boundary_fit$convergence
boundary_fit$inference_available
vcov(boundary_fit)
```

The returned starting coefficients are diagnostic values, not maximum likelihood
estimates. Wald covariance is unavailable, and `logLik()`, `AIC()` and `BIC()`
refuse this comparison. In a grouped model, perfect within-group alignment can
also produce an unbounded likelihood. A zero-concentration boundary and singular
information are separate conditions; inspect the reported `fit_status` rather
than treating every large or small concentration as the same failure.

## Keep rows aligned when values are missing

```{r}
with_missing <- dat
with_missing$y[3] <- NA
fit_exclude <- circular_regression(
  y ~ x1 + x2:z2, with_missing, reference = "x1", na.action = na.exclude
)
length(fitted(fit_exclude))
is.na(fitted(fit_exclude)[3])
```

`na.exclude` restores omitted rows in in-sample fitted values, residuals and
predictions. New-data prediction rejects missing or nonfinite covariates.
For grouped fits, provide original or retained group identifiers; the fitter
uses the same row alignment as the response and covariates.
